I've had mine for about a year. It has excellent features and with some patience you can configure it for games you wouldn't expect any gamepad to work for. The d-pad is maybe the most annoying part, requiring a lot of pressure in some corners and not as much in others. I never map gameplay to that, only menu stuff. The right-pad takes the place of a right-analogue stick on other controllers, so it takes the most getting used to. You'll drift your thumb over it accidentally sometimes getting a reaction like you bumped the stick (throwing the camera around or whatever you've mapped). But it offers a lot of new options too, giving you the ability to treat it like a stick or a mouse pointer as the game requires.

The only element of the controller that seems low quality to me, is the main vibration motor. It is loud. Since I play with headphones, my wife get amused by the buzzing coming from my hands cause its all she hears. I've yet to load batteries into it, so perhaps they dampen the sound (seems reasonable they would), but its always been convenient to play with it wired so far.

Anyway, hope you enjoy it. I have.

All that said, I keep an xbox one controller around for certain games where I just need that two-stick feel. The X1 controller is fantastic, has generally perfect support in all PC games, and is well worth the price for the official versions. It's build quality and consistency is second to none. I've never had a bad one.

what part of bitcoin's structure keeps a finite amount in existence?
Or is it that it gets so hard to mine that there is theoretically a cap?

The number of coins created per block mined is programmed to cut in half over a set schedule until no more coins are produced.

When no more coins are minted each block, the only incentive to mine will be transaction fees.

The creator made it that way.

Every time a new block is found/mined, a certain number of Bitcoin are generated. After 210,000 blocks are found, the rate reduces to 50% of what it was for when a new block is found. It goes down another 50% at 420,000, etc. etc.

Now due to that math thingy that says you can cut things in half forever without reaching zero if your numeric resolution is sufficient it never really reaches 0 BTC per block, but it does from a practical perspective.
It is hardcoded into the mining network. It could theoretically be changed if there was a change in the code, and a majority of the miners accepted the update.
